note: Odysseus sleeps under the olive bushes (end of Book 5). Athena goes to the Phaeacian city. The narrator gives the backstory: the Phaeacians lived in Hypereia near the Cyclopes, who harmed them. Nausithous moved them to Scheria, built a wall, houses and temples, and divided the land. He is dead, and Alcinous rules. Athena goes to the chamber of Nausicaa, who sleeps between two handmaids at the doorposts. She rushes like a breath of wind to the bed, takes the likeness of the daughter of Dymas, and begins to speak (25). Findings: 1-2: the transition formula "ὣς ὁ μὲν … αὐτὰρ Ἀθήνη" joins Book 5 and Book 6. Zenodotus accented καθεῦδε (scholion H.P.). | 2 ἀρημένος: defective participle, origin disputed. The lexicon records it; no article. | 3: scholion E says the Phaeacian land is "what is now called Corcyra". Lead for corcyra-and-the-phaeacians. | 4 Ὑπερείῃ: not the Thessalian spring of the existing hypereia. Scholia: Camarina in Sicily, or an island near the Cyclopes. New id hypereia-of-the-phaeacians. | 8 ἀλφηστάων: "grain-eating" in the translation; scholion H glosses "inventive, provident". Keep both in the term article. | 11 κηρί (doom) and 158 κῆρι (heart) need accent-sensitive patterns. | 12 μήδεα "counsels" is a homograph of μήδεα "genitals" (129). Lexicon only. | 14, 17 μεγαλήτωρ: the great-hearted article names the word but has no pattern. | 16: "like the immortal goddesses in build and in looks" is a variant of the like-the-goddesses formula, not the same phrase. | 18-19: the two handmaids at the doorposts are a visit-scene detail. | 20: short simile ἀνέμου ὡς πνοιή (ὡς placed inside the phrase; lexicon note). | 22 ναυσικλειτοῖο Δύμαντος: Dymas is a homonym of Hecuba's father (Iliad 16.718). Use a qualified id. | Translation check: no defects found. 19 "the shining doors were closed" for ἐπέκειντο is acceptable.

Athena's speech in the dream. Nausicaa's clothes lie unwashed, her marriage is near, and the best Phaeacians court her. She must ask her father for the mules and the wagon to take the clothes to the washing pits far from the city. Athena returns to Olympus, which the narrator describes: never shaken by wind, wet by rain or touched by snow, under a cloudless sky and a white gleam. Dawn wakes Nausicaa, who wonders at the dream and goes to tell her parents. Findings: 27-28 ἄγωνται: plural; the groom's escort or the groom's family. The translation keeps the ambiguity ("those who will lead you home"). | 29 φάτις: the scholia lemma reads ἀνθρώπων, Murray prints ἀνθρώπους; a Callistratus note follows. Minor; record in phemis. | 31 ἅμʼ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφι (-φι ending), 36 ἠῶθι πρό, 48 Ἠὼς ἐΰθρονος: three dawn expressions, none matched by dawn-line. | 32 συνέριθος: rare word, lexicon only. | 37 ἄμαξα and 57 ἀπήνη: the translation renders ἄμαξα "wagon" and ἀπήνη "carriage" with one lapse at 72 ("mule wagon" for ἄμαξαν ἡμιονείην, correct). Consistent. One article "wagon" for both words. | 38 ζῶστρα, πέπλοι, ῥήγεα: sashes, robes, coverlets. πέπλος goes to robe; ῥήγεα gets a low-priority article. | 42 φασί "they say": the narrator distances himself from the description. Note in olympus. | 42 θεῶν ἕδος ἀσφαλὲς αἰεί: shared with Hesiod, Theogony 117-118, 128. New formula seat-firm-forever. | 44 αἴθρη: Rhianus read αἰθήρ; 46 τῷ ἔνι: Rhianus read τῇ ἔνι (scholia H.P.). | 42-46: imitated by Lucretius 3.18-24 and echoed by Tennyson. | 48 ἐΰθρονος: scholion E.P.V. takes θρόνος as Dawn's chariot seat; the lexicon also cites "flowered" (θρόνα). Put the dispute in of-the-fair-throne. | 49 ὄνειρον is wrongly claimed by the god Dream (Iliad 2). Move to onar; add except to dream.

Nausicaa finds her mother at the hearth, spinning sea-purple wool with her women, and meets her father as he goes to the council of kings. She asks "Papa dear" for the high wagon, giving her father's and brothers' need of clean clothes as the reason. She is ashamed to name her marriage, but her father understands everything and orders the slaves to make the wagon ready. The mules are yoked and the clothes are loaded. Findings: 53 ἠλάκατα στρωφῶσʼ ἁλιπόρφυρα: spinning, not weaving; new articles distaff and sea-purple. | 54 κλειτοὺς βασιλῆας: famous has only κλειτῶν; kings matches βασιλῆας. | 57 πάππα φίλʼ: unique address; treated in fathers-and-daughters. | 62-63: five sons, two married (ὀπυίοντες), three unmarried (ἠίθεοι). New people entry sons-of-alcinous. | 66 αἴδετο: aidos patterns miss this form. | 69, 71 δμῶες, δμώεσσιν: male slaves. No pattern anywhere. Extend doulios. | 70 ὑπερτερίῃ ἀραρυῖαν "fitted with an upper frame": the sense of ὑπερτερίη (box or awning) is uncertain. Treat in wagon. | 74-75: Aristophanes of Byzantium read φέρον and κατέθηκαν (subject: the slaves), scholion H.P. | 75 ἐυξέστῳ: extend polished (ἐΰξοος) to the synonym ἐΰξεστος. | Translation check: 53 "turning the sea-purple wool on her distaff" is correct; ἠλάκατα is the wool on the distaff.

The mother packs food, relishes and wine in a goatskin, and gives Nausicaa olive oil in a golden flask. Nausicaa drives the mules to the river. At the ever-flowing pits the girls loose the mules to graze, tread the clothes in the trenches in competition, and spread them on the shingle. They bathe, anoint themselves, eat by the river, and then throw off their veils to play ball. Findings: 79, 215 λήκυθος: the only λήκυθος in Homer. Treat in olive-oil. | 80 χυτλώσαιτο: "bathe and anoint"; the translation "anoint herself after bathing" keeps both. | 82 μάστιξεν δʼ ἐλάαν: head of the chariot-journey formula; καναχή ἡμιόνοιιν is a dual. | 86 ἐπηετανοί, 87 ὑπεκπρόρεεν: the lexicon explains the triple compound. | 89 πάρα: Aristarchus accented with anastrophe (scholion). | 90 τρώγειν and 318 τρώχων are falsely claimed by trojans (Τρώ*; fixed in the index audit with !τρωγ* and !τρωχ*). Add exclusions. | 90 μελιηδέα: a different word from honey-sweet (μελίφρων). New low-priority epithet. | 92 ἔριδα προφέρουσαι: the good, competitive ἔρις. Extend eris; link hesiods-two-strifes. | 96 λίπʼ ἐλαίῳ: λίπα, an old case form; the bathing pattern already matches. | 100 σφαίρῃ ταὶ δʼ ἄρʼ: Aristarchus's reading; πᾶσαι is reported for other copies. Record in ball-play. | 100 κρήδεμνα: veil names κρήδεμνον as an alias only. Add the form. | Reception: Athenaeus 1.14d-15 (ball games, Agallis of Corcyra), 1.20f (Sophocles played ball as Nausicaa); Eustathius names the Πλύντριαι.

Nausicaa leads the song and dance and stands out among her maids like Artemis among the nymphs on Taygetus or Erymanthus. Athena plans that Odysseus will wake. Nausicaa throws the ball, misses a maid, and the ball falls into a deep eddy. The girls shout, and Odysseus wakes. He asks whether the people are violent or hospitable, and whether the cry came from nymphs or from humans who speak. Findings: 101 ἤρχετο μολπῆς: "began the song and dance"; μολπή is not matched by dance. | 102 κατʼ οὔρεα: the scholia report κατʼ οὔρεος as the vulgate and οὔρεα as "better"; Murray prints οὔρεα. | 103 Τηΰγετον: Ionic form; new places taygetus and erymanthus. A scholion explains that Homer gives Artemis boars and deer, not lions, citing Aristotle (Historia animalium 6.31). | 104 κάπροισι, ἐλάφοισι: boar and deer patterns miss these forms. | 105 κοῦραι Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο: the nymphs article already cites Od. 6.105. | 106 ἀγρονόμοι: treat in nymphs. | 108 ἀριγνώτη and 300 ἀρίγνωτʼ: a verbal echo (Artemis among nymphs, the house among houses). | 112 ἄλλʼ ἐνόησε θεά: plot-turning formula; again at 251. | 115 βασίλεια "the princess": acceptable for a king's daughter. Extend basileus with the feminine. | 119-121 = 9.175-176 = 13.200-202: new formula article to-the-land-of-what-mortals. | 122 ὥς τε: "as if" (the translation) or exclamatory "how". 124 = Iliad 20.9. Modern editors suspected 123-124. New note the-nymphs-cry-122-124. | 122 ἀυτή: a non-martial cry; aute misses the form.

Odysseus breaks off a leafy branch to cover himself and comes out like a rain-beaten mountain lion driven by hunger. The girls flee; only Nausicaa stands, given courage by Athena. Odysseus weighs whether to clasp her knees or to speak from a distance, and chooses soothing words. He begins: "I beseech you, queen: are you a goddess or a mortal?" Findings: 129 μήδεα φωτός: "genitals" (μῆδος B); homograph of 12. | 130-136: the lion simile shares its opening and 134 with Iliad 12.299-306 (Sarpedon). New simile the-lion-and-the-girls plus a cross-reference in the-mountain-lion-and-the-fold. | 133 γαστήρ: first instance of the belly motif. Low-priority term gaster. | 137 σμερδαλέος: Zenodotus read ἀργαλέος; λευγαλέος is also reported and rejected (scholion H.P.). | 138 τρέσσαν: Aristarchus held that τρεῖν means "flee". Pausanias 1.22.6 records Polygnotus's painting of this scene. | 141-147: decision scene; 145 = Iliad 13.458. Athenocles suspected 144 as redundant. | 147 γοῦνα and 149 γουνοῦμαι: gounata and supplication miss these forms. | 148 μειλίχιον καὶ κερδαλέον: kerdos already cites this line. | 149 γουνοῦμαί σε "I beseech you": the Greek means "I clasp your knees" while he stands apart. The lexicon note says so; the English loses the figure. Consider "I clasp your knees in prayer" or a note. | 149 ἦ βροτός: Ptolemy of Ascalon read it as a question (circumflex); others as "either god or mortal" (scholion P). New formula god-or-mortal.

Odysseus likens Nausicaa to Artemis and calls her parents, brothers and future husband blessed. He compares his wonder to the wonder he felt at a young palm by Apollo's altar on Delos, where he once came with an army. He tells her he escaped the sea yesterday, after twenty days from Ogygia, and asks for pity. Findings: 151, 323 Διὸς κούρῃ μεγάλοιο: not matched by daughter-of-zeus. | 154-159 τρὶς μάκαρες … μακάρτατος: makarismos. New formula thrice-blessed. | 155 τρὶς μάκαρες δέ: δέ in third position (Merry-Riddell). | 156 ἐυφροσύνῃσιν: variant ἐν εὐφροσύνῃσιν rejected in the scholia. Minor. | 157 θάλος: metaphor that prepares the palm simile; εἰσοιχνεῦσαν is feminine by sense. | 158 περὶ κῆρι: adverbial "above all" or "in his heart". The translation gives both ("in his heart, far above all others"). | 159 ἐέδνοισι βρίσας: bride-price misses ἐέδνοισι. | 162-169: Delos, Apollo's altar, the palm (φοῖνιξ, homograph of purple and Phoenix). Reception: Cicero, De legibus 1.2 and Pliny NH 16.240 say the palm was still shown; Hymn to Apollo 117 (Leto and the palm). | 166 ἐτεθήπεα, 168 τέθηπα: the θάμβος root; thambos misses the forms. | 167 δόρυ "stem": the sense "tree trunk", not "spear". The spear article must not claim it (it does not). | 170 ἐεικοστῷ: twentieth day since leaving Ogygia (17 days of sailing + 2 nights and days in the sea, 5.278-279, 5.388). | 172 Ὠγυγίης: new place ogygia. | 175 ἄνασσα, ἐλέαιρε: anax (feminine) and pity.

Odysseus asks Nausicaa to show him the town and give him a rag. He wishes her a husband, a home and like-mindedness, for nothing is better than a man and wife of one mind. Nausicaa answers that Zeus deals out prosperity as he wishes and that the stranger will not lack clothes. She names the Phaeacians and her father, and calls her fleeing maids back. Findings: 177-178: the translation distinguishes ἄστυ "town" from πόλις "city"; polis has only πόλιν. | 179 εἴλυμα σπείρων: σπεῖρον "cloth" here, σπεῖρα "rigging" at 269. Lexicon only. | 181-185: ὁμοφροσύνη; 183 dual ὁμοφρονέοντε, ἔχητον. 185 ἔκλυον: "they know it best" (the translation) or "they are best spoken of". New term homophrosyne and saying nothing-better-than-like-mindedness. | 186 ἀντίον ηὔδα: variant of then-answered. | 187-191: anacoluthon; the thought resumes at 191 νῦν δʼ, ἐπεί. The translation marks the break with a semicolon. | 188-190 ὄλβος: new term olbos and saying zeus-deals-out-prosperity. | 193 ἱκέτην ταλαπείριον: new epithet much-tried; ἱκέτης goes to supplication. The construction of ὧν … ἀντιάσαντα is disputed (lexicon). | 197 ἐκ … ἔχεται "depends on": lexicon. | 200 ἦ μή: question expecting "no".

Nausicaa tells the maids that no living mortal will come to the Phaeacians as an enemy, since they are dear to the gods and live far off in the sea. The stranger is an unlucky wanderer; strangers and beggars come from Zeus. The maids seat him in shelter, give him a cloak, a tunic and oil, and tell him to bathe. Odysseus asks them to stand apart, because he is ashamed to strip among the girls. Findings: 201 διερός: Aristarchus "living"; Callistratus read δυερός "wretched"; a gloss gives "hostile, raider", which Lehrs ascribes to Aristarchus. New term dieros. | 203: Athenaeus 1.16e quotes "very dear to the immortals". Treat in phaeacians. | 204 πολυκλύστῳ, 205 ἔσχατοι: remoteness of the Phaeacians. | 207 κομέειν: Callistratus read τῷ (scholion H). | 207-208: repeated by Eumaeus at 14.57-58. New saying strangers-and-beggars-are-from-zeus; new term ptochos. | 209 βρῶσίν τε πόσιν τε: πόσιν "drink" is falsely claimed by posis (husband). Add except for 209, 246, 248. | 214 φᾶρος: cloak already matches. | 219-220 ἀπολούσομαι, χρίσομαι: short-vowel subjunctives or futures; lexicon. | 221-222 αἰδέομαι γυμνοῦσθαι: reversal of the guest-bath scene; new theme nakedness; aidos note.

Odysseus washes the brine off and dresses. Athena makes him taller and sturdier and gives him curling hair like the hyacinth, pouring grace on him as a craftsman pours gold over silver. He sits on the shore, shining. Nausicaa tells her maids that he must have come by the will of the gods, wishes that such a man could be her husband, and tells them to feed him. He eats greedily. Findings: 226 ἁλὸς χνόον ἀτρυγέτοιο: barren-sea matches. | 229-235: divine beautification; 232-235 = 23.159-162. New theme divine-beautification and simile gold-poured-on-silver. | 231 οὔλας κόμας, ὑακινθίνῳ ἄνθει: curly hair, like the hyacinth (cluster or color). thick-and-woolly and hair miss the forms. | 239 κλῦτέ μευ: plural form of the hear-me formula; λευκώλενοι used of servants, the only such use. | 240 οὐ πάντων ἀέκητι θεῶν: litotes. | 241 ἀντιθέοισι: of the Phaeacians. | 242 δέατʼ: found only here; Aristarchus read δόατʼ. New note deato-or-doato. | 244-245: Aristarchus obelized both lines and doubted 244 because Alcman adapted it. Plutarch (De audiendis poetis 27a-b) blames the wish; Ephorus praised it (scholion Q.T.). New note nausicaas-wish-244-245. | 244 πόσις "husband", 246 and 248 πόσιν "drink": the homograph again. | 249 πολύτλας: much-enduring lacks the pattern.

Nausicaa folds the clothes, yokes the mules and tells Odysseus how to come to the city. He is to walk with the maids behind the wagon through the fields. She describes the city: a high wall, a harbor on each side, a narrow entrance, the ships drawn up each on its berth, the agora around the Posideion, and the Phaeacians busy with ships and oars, not bows. She fears the talk of the townsmen. Findings: 254 ἔπος τʼ ἔφατʼ ἔκ τʼ ὀνόμαζεν: translated "called him by name". Nausicaa does not know his name and calls him ξεῖνε (255). The lexicon glosses ὀνόμαζεν "addressed". Translation fix needed: "and spoke to him and addressed him". The formula pattern also misses the form with final ν. | 258 ἀπινύσσειν: rare; lexicon. | 262-272: anacoluthon; the main clause after ἐπὴν … ἐπιβήομεν never comes. The translation keeps the break. | 264 εἰσίθμη: hapax; Aristophanes read ἴσθμη (scholion B.H.Q.). | 265 ἐπίστιον: the lexicon glosses "berth", the translation "ship-shed". Settle one gloss in the term article and align. | 266 Ποσιδήιον: "shrine of Poseidon" in the translation, "precinct" in the lexicon. Fine; new place posideion. | 267 ῥυτοῖσιν λάεσσι: hauled stones (Od. 14.10); λάεσσι is not claimed by Laas. | 268 μελαινάων, 269 ἐρετμά, 270 βιός, φαρέτρη, 271 ἱστοί, ἐῖσαι, 272 πολιήν: none matched by the existing patterns. | 273 φῆμιν ἀδευκέα: new term phemis. | 275: start of the fourteen lines (275-288) athetized in the scholia.

Nausicaa quotes the imagined gossip: who is this tall stranger, a castaway or a god come at her prayer; she scorns the Phaeacians who woo her. She says she would blame any girl who mixed with men before a public marriage. She tells Odysseus to wait in Athena's poplar grove, near her father's estate, a shout's distance from the city, and then to ask for the house of Alcinous, which even a child could show him. Findings: 276-285: τις-speech by an imagined "baser man" (275). tis-speech misses τις εἴπῃσι. | 278 ἦ: Murray's accent "surely"; some print ἤ … ἤ "either … or". | 278 νηός "ship" (genitive): ships matches it correctly; temple must not take νηός. | 280 πολυάρητος: new low-priority epithet. | 282 βέλτερον: sarcastic. | 286 νεμεσῶ: nemesis matches. | 287: Aristarchus read ἠδʼ for ἥ τʼ (scholion Q). Minor. | 288 ἀμφάδιον γάμον: marriage patterns catch nothing in the book. | 289: Aristarchus read σὺ δʼ ὦκʼ ἐμέθεν; 290 Zenodotus ἐμέειο. | 290 πομπῆς καὶ νόστοιο: new term pompe; nostos misses the forms. | 291-294: grove of Athena (poplars, spring, meadow), the τέμενος of Alcinous; new formula within-shouting-distance. | 297 δώματʼ ἀφῖχθαι: Aristophanes's reading reported (scholion H). 298 ἐρέεσθαι: γρ. ἔρχεσθαι.

Nausicaa describes the house: Odysseus must pass through the hall to her mother, who sits at the hearth in the firelight, spinning sea-purple wool against a pillar, with the father's throne beside her. He must pass the king and clasp the queen's knees. Nausicaa drives off; she drives with care so that the walkers can keep up. At sunset they reach the grove, and Odysseus prays to Athena. Findings: 301 νήπιος "infant": the literal sense; nepios matches. | 303 ἥρωος: Alcinous called ἥρως. | 305: a scholion explains ἐπʼ ἐσχάρῃ as "at the hearth" on a raised seat. | 306 θαῦμα ἰδέσθαι: thambos note. | 307 δμωαί: Murray prints no iota subscript, so handmaids ("=δμῳ*") misses it. | 308 αὐτῇ: the pillar, the hearth or the queen; lexicon. Treat in house-of-alcinous. | 309 ἀθάνατος ὥς: short comparison; treat in alcinous. | 310-315: supplication of the queen; a scholion explains why the queen and not the king (woman to woman, or Arete's wisdom; Callistratus "the female is pitiful"). | 311 νόστιμον ἦμαρ: new formula day-of-homecoming. | 315 σὴν ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν: variant for dear-native-land. | 318 πλίσσοντο: disputed; Callistratus read τρεχέτην; τρώχων falsely matched by trojans (fixed in the index audit). | 321 δύσετό τʼ ἠέλιος: sunset-lines misses it. 322 ἱρόν: hieros misses it. | 324 Ἀτρυτώνη: derivation uncertain; atrytone matches.

Odysseus reproaches Athena for not hearing him when Poseidon shattered him and asks to come to the Phaeacians dear and pitied. Athena hears, but does not yet appear to him face to face, out of respect for her father's brother, who stays angry until Odysseus reaches his own land. Findings: 326 ῥαιομένου … ἔρραιε: the verb repeated; κλυτὸς ἐννοσίγαιος. | 327 = Iliad 24.309 (Priam's prayer). New formula dear-and-pitied. ἐλεεινόν is not matched by pity. | 328 = the prayer-closing line; prayer-type-scene. | 329 αἴδετο: variant ἄζετο (scholion P). Respect, not shame: aidos note. | 330 πατροκασίγνητον: kasignetos misses the compound. Aristarchus put a circumflex on ἐπιζαφελῶς; the scholion says it should be barytone. | 331 ἀντιθέῳ: antitheos misses the form. The wrath of Poseidon is foreshadowed to the end of the poem: new story the-wrath-of-poseidon.
